You start from a template, swap in your own text and photos, and export the result, which cuts out most of the layout decisions that make design software hard to learn. It covers social media posts, presentations, flyers, resumes, posters, short videos, whiteboards, and simple websites in one editor. A built-in library of photos, graphics, fonts, and music means most projects can be finished without leaving the app.

item.title: Causal
item.description:
Causal was created for finance teams that outgrew spreadsheets. Users build models from blocks that represent revenue, headcount, and costs, link them to data from accounting and CRM systems, and see results as charts and dashboards. The structure makes models easier to follow and share than a sprawling workbook.

Scenario planning is a core strength. Teams can change assumptions, such as hiring plans or pricing, and compare outcomes side by side, then present the results to executives and investors. AI features help create models from descriptions and explain changes in numbers.

item.title: ChatGPT
item.description: ChatGPT is a chat interface to OpenAI’s language models. You type or speak a request and it answers in plain language, whether that means drafting an email, explaining a concept, debugging a function, or summarizing a long PDF. It can take images and files as input and generate images in return. For many people it is the first AI tool they ever used, and that familiarity is a big part of why it remains the default comparison for every other assistant.

item.title: Civitai
item.description:
Civitai is where much of the open-source image generation community meets. Creators upload checkpoints, LoRAs, embeddings, and other add-ons for Stable Diffusion, FLUX, and related models, together with sample images and the prompts used. Others download them to run locally in tools like ComfyUI or Automatic1111, or try them in the browser. Ratings, comments, and example galleries make it easier to judge a model before downloading.

The site offers more than a library. Users can generate images on Civitai’s servers using credits, train their own LoRAs from a set of images, and take part in challenges and bounties that reward creators. Articles and guides share techniques, and a point system pays for the use of the site’s services. It became the unofficial catalog for community-trained styles, characters, and concepts.

item.title: Cleanup.pictures
item.description:
Cleanup.pictures does one thing with minimal effort. Upload a photo, brush over a stranger in the background, a power line, a logo, or a blemish, and the tool removes it and fills the gap with a plausible background. Results come back within seconds and can be downloaded, which makes it a quick fix for product photos, real estate listings, travel pictures, and social media posts.

It works well on simple backgrounds such as sky, grass, walls, and water, and less well when the removed object sits in front of detailed patterns, faces, or text that the model would have to invent. For larger images, a higher-resolution output is available on paid plans. The same kind of inpainting appears in other tools, including Clipdrop, which offers a related cleanup feature, along with Photoshop’s Generative Fill and Remove tool and the Magic Eraser on Google Pixel phones.

item.title: Climate FieldView
item.description:
Climate FieldView helps farmers use their data. With a device plugged into farm equipment, FieldView Drive collects information about planting, applications, and harvest, and the data syncs to the cloud, where farmers view maps of their fields, compare hybrids and practices, and analyze yield. Satellite imagery tracks crop health during the season, and weather data and field notes add context.

Advanced features support planning. Variable-rate prescriptions tell equipment to apply seed and fertilizer at different rates across a field based on zones, which can improve efficiency, and scripts or models estimate the profitability of decisions. Integrations with equipment and other agriculture software reduce manual data transfers. Machine learning supports yield predictions and recommendations.

item.title: Climate TRACE
item.description: Climate TRACE exists because official emissions reporting is slow and incomplete. The coalition combines satellite images, sensor data, and public records and applies machine learning to estimate emissions from individual sources: power plants, steel mills, oil and gas fields, ships, aircraft, cement plants, farms, and more. The result is a global inventory that can be searched by country, sector, or even a single facility, updated more frequently than government reports.

item.title: ComfyUI
item.description: ComfyUI gives you precise control over generative AI by showing the whole pipeline. Instead of a prompt box and a button, you assemble a graph: load a model, encode a prompt, set up a sampler, add LoRAs or ControlNet for guidance, upscale, and save. Each step is a node you can inspect and rewire. It started with Stable Diffusion and now supports many image, video, and audio models, including FLUX, so new models are often usable in ComfyUI first.

item.title: CoreWeave
item.description:
CoreWeave began as a company mining cryptocurrency and turned its GPU capacity into a cloud for AI. Customers rent clusters of NVIDIA GPUs for training and running models, with networking and storage built for large workloads. Because it specializes, it can often deploy new GPU generations quickly.

The platform runs on Kubernetes and offers managed services for training, inference, and storage. Major AI labs and big technology companies have signed large contracts, and the company has built or leased data centers around the world. It acquired Weights & Biases to add developer tooling to its infrastructure.

item.title: Coze
item.description:
Coze lets non-programmers build conversational agents. In its editor, you describe the bot’s role and behavior, choose a language model, and attach tools: plugins for web search, image generation, and other services, plus knowledge bases that hold your documents. Visual workflows chain steps together for more complex tasks, and memory features let a bot recall details about users. A store lets creators share and discover bots built by others.

Publishing is flexible. A finished agent can be deployed to messaging apps and chat platforms, embedded on a website, or exposed through an API, which makes it practical for customer support, community bots, personal assistants, and internal tools. ByteDance has also released parts of the platform as open source for those who want to run it themselves, and offers separate editions for different regions.

item.title: Craiyon
item.description:
Craiyon began as DALL-E mini, an open-source experiment that went viral for producing odd, low-resolution images from text prompts. It was one of the first image generators many people tried, and it popularized the idea that anyone could make pictures with words. The site then rebranded as Craiyon and kept its low barrier to entry: open the page, type a prompt, and wait for the results.

The quality has improved with newer models, and Craiyon now produces more detailed images in several styles, including photos, illustrations, and drawings. Paid plans remove ads, speed up generation, and add features such as faster queues, higher resolution, and a private mode. The tool is positioned for casual use, like quick illustrations, memes, and idea sketches, instead of professional production.

item.title: Decktopus
item.description: Decktopus is built for people who need a presentation quickly. You enter a topic or a short brief, answer a few questions about the audience and goal, and the AI produces an outline and a deck of designed slides with suggested images and speaker notes. You then edit the text and layout in a drag-and-drop editor. It also offers templates for pitches, reports, and sales decks, and a brand kit for colors and logos.

item.title: Domo AI
item.description:
Domo aims to put an organization’s data in one place. It connects to hundreds of sources, from databases and spreadsheets to marketing and finance platforms, and lets users clean and combine data and then build dashboards and reports. Business users can view metrics on the web or mobile and set alerts, and developers can build custom apps on top of the data.

AI is built through the product. Users can ask questions in natural language and receive charts and answers, models can forecast and detect anomalies, and AI agents and workflows can automate tasks, such as summarizing reports or triggering actions when numbers change. Domo also lets companies connect their own models, and offers governance features for data access.

item.title: Dream by WOMBO
item.description: Dream by WOMBO is aimed at casual creators who want to see their ideas as art without learning prompt techniques. You type a phrase, pick a style such as oil painting, anime, fantasy, or neon, and the app returns an image in a few seconds. The style menu does much of the work that detailed prompts would do in other tools, which makes it approachable on a phone. It is popular for profile pictures, wallpapers, and quick social posts.

item.title: Durable
item.description:
Durable promises a website with minimal effort. You tell it the kind of business you run and where you are, and it builds a site with pages, copy, images, and a layout in under a minute, which you can then edit with simple controls. It’s aimed at freelancers and local service businesses, such as plumbers, photographers, and consultants, who need an online presence quickly.

Beyond the site, Durable includes small-business tools. A built-in CRM tracks leads and customers, an invoicing feature handles billing, and AI assistants help write blog posts, social content, and marketing copy. It offers hosting and a custom domain, and basic analytics. Everything lives in one account, so owners avoid piecing together several services.

item.title: FarmLogs
item.description:
FarmLogs began as a way for farmers to keep records digitally instead of in notebooks. Growers could map their fields, log planting, spraying, and harvest activities, track inputs and costs, and see weather and satellite imagery for each field. The aim was to make it easier to understand what was working in a season, to meet record-keeping requirements, and to share information with advisors and landlords.

The product became part of Bushel, a company that provides software for grain buyers, farmers, and the supply chain. Under the name Bushel Farm, it connects farmers with grain markets and elevators, shows contract and delivery information, and supports tools for tracking grain inventory. Data from fields and grain marketing is brought into one view, and analytics help evaluate profitability.

item.title: Fashwell
item.description:
Fashwell works on a persistent problem in online retail: product data is often incomplete or inconsistent. Its AI looks at product photos and automatically identifies attributes such as category, color, pattern, shape, neckline, and material, creating detailed, standardized tags. Those tags help retailers organize catalogs, improve search, and power filters that match how customers describe items.

The same technology supports discovery features. Visual search lets shoppers find similar items from an image, recommendation systems suggest products that match a style, and outfit and style-matching tools help shoppers complete a look. Retailers use it to save the effort of manual tagging across thousands of items and to improve the consistency of information across channels.

item.title: Fliki
item.description:
Fliki turns written content into video. A user pastes a script, links an article, or writes a prompt, and the tool splits it into scenes, picks visuals from a stock library or generated media, and adds narration with a synthetic voice. The editor allows swapping clips, adjusting text, and changing voices.

A big draw is the range of voices and languages, which lets creators produce the same video in several markets. Avatars and voice cloning are available, and text to speech is offered as a standalone product for narration and audio. Marketers, educators, and YouTubers use it to repurpose content.

item.title: FlutterFlow
item.description: FlutterFlow combines the speed of a visual builder with real code. You design screens by dragging widgets, define logic with a visual action editor, and connect to backends such as Firebase, Supabase, or any API. Because it generates Flutter code, apps run natively on iOS and Android and also on the web, and you can export the code to continue development in a standard IDE, which avoids the lock-in of many no-code tools.

item.title: Framer
item.description:
Framer started as a prototyping tool and became a full website builder. Designers lay out pages on a canvas much like they do in Figma, set up responsive behavior, add animations and interactions, and publish to a fast hosted site with a custom domain. Because it gives designers precise control over visuals and motion, it’s popular for portfolios, landing pages, and marketing sites.

A CMS manages blog posts and other structured content, and features for SEO, localization, and analytics support production sites. AI tools generate a first draft of a site from a description, create wireframes, and write copy, which speeds up the start of a project. Components and code overrides allow customization when needed, and a marketplace of templates and plugins helps.

item.title: Freepik AI
item.description: Freepik began as a stock site for vectors, photos, and icons, and many designers already knew it. It has added a full AI suite on top. The image generator creates pictures from text prompts, and tools for editing, upscaling, retouching, and expanding images let users refine them. Video generation and animation features turn stills or prompts into short clips, and a workspace organizes projects and lets you mix different tools.

item.title: Gamma
item.description:
Gamma reimagined the presentation. Instead of slides built from a blank template, you describe what you want, such as a pitch for a new product or a lesson on photosynthesis, and Gamma generates a complete, designed deck with text, layouts, and images. The format uses flexible cards that expand and collapse, so presentations can feel more like interactive documents, and it also produces documents and one-page websites.

Editing is conversational and visual. You can ask the AI to rewrite a section, change the style, add images, or restructure, or edit manually with simple controls. Themes keep designs consistent, brand settings apply company fonts and colors, and sharing by link includes analytics on who viewed it. Decks can be exported to PowerPoint or PDF, and it integrates with other tools.

item.title: Gemini
item.description: Gemini is Google’s family of AI models and the assistant built on top of them. You can use it in the standalone Gemini app and website, but it also shows up inside the products many people already use: it can help draft emails in Gmail, rewrite text in Docs, summarize files in Drive, and answer questions on Android phones. If most of your work and personal life already runs on a Google account, that integration is the main reason to choose Gemini over another assistant.

item.title: Gen-2
item.description:
Runway builds generative video tools for filmmakers, designers, and creators. Gen-3 Alpha was a major step in its line, generating short clips from a text prompt or an image with better detail, motion, and consistency than earlier versions. It supported controls for camera movement and style.

Runway’s platform around its models includes editing tools, motion brush features, and ways to extend or modify clips. Its research focuses on world models and video generation for creative work, and the company works with studios and artists. The newer models in the line have largely taken the place of Gen-3.

item.title: Generated Photos
item.description:
Generated Photos solves a licensing problem: real people’s faces carry privacy and consent obligations, and stock photos can be expensive or restrictive. Its library holds images of faces created by generative models, which depict nobody in particular. Designers use them for website and app mockups, marketers for illustrations, and developers for placeholder avatars in user interfaces.

Several tools extend the library. A face generator lets you pick attributes such as age, gender, ethnicity, hair, and emotion and create new faces, and a photo anonymizer replaces a real face in a picture with a synthetic one. Datasets of synthetic faces serve machine learning teams who need varied images without privacy concerns, and an API provides access for automated use. Full-body and other synthetic image options have been added.

item.title: GetIMG.ai
item.description: getimg.ai provides a web workspace for creating and editing images with AI. You can generate pictures from a prompt using a choice of models, including Stable Diffusion variants and other leading generators, then refine them. Tools for inpainting let you replace part of an image, outpainting extends it past its borders, and an infinite canvas allows you to compose scenes from several generations. Upscaling, background removal, and face tools help finish the result.

item.title: Google Maps
item.description: Google Maps is the default map for much of the world. It provides turn-by-turn navigation with live traffic and rerouting, public transit schedules, walking and cycling directions, and detailed maps with business hours, photos, reviews, and popular times. Street View lets you look at places at ground level, Live View uses your phone’s camera to show directions as arrows in the real world, and offline maps work without a connection.

item.title: Heptabase
item.description: Heptabase treats notes as cards that you place on whiteboards, group, and connect. Instead of a long document or a folder tree, you build up an understanding of a topic visually: a card for each idea, laid out next to related ones, with arrows and sections that show structure. It suits people who learn and plan by seeing the relationships among ideas, such as researchers, students, writers, and product thinkers.

item.title: Homestyler
item.description:
Homestyler makes home design accessible. You draw a floor plan or start from a template, add walls, doors, and windows, and then furnish rooms from a catalog of real products and styles. A 3D view lets you walk through the space, and realistic renderings show how finishes and lighting would look. Homeowners use it to plan renovations and arrange furniture, and designers use it to present ideas to clients.

AI features speed up design. Tools can generate interior styles from a photo of a room, suggest layouts, and produce renderings from a simple description, and some features let you scan or upload a room as a starting point. Community galleries share designs for inspiration, and links to retailers make it easier to buy items you have selected.

item.title: Houzz
item.description:
Houzz started as a place to browse home photos and save ideas. Users look through millions of images of kitchens, bathrooms, gardens, and living rooms, save them to idea books, and find the products and professionals behind them. A directory lists architects, designers, and contractors with reviews and portfolios, so homeowners can contact people who match their taste and budget.

The platform includes a marketplace for furniture, lighting, and home goods, with augmented reality features that show how an item might look in your room. For professionals, Houzz Pro is software for managing leads, estimates, invoices, projects, and client communication, with tools to showcase their work. AI features help with design suggestions, image search, and automating parts of the business workflow.

item.title: Infogram
item.description:
Infogram helps turn numbers into visual stories. You choose a template for an infographic, report, chart, or dashboard, import data from a spreadsheet or connect to a live source, and customize the design with your brand colors and fonts. The tool produces polished charts and maps, many of them interactive, that can be embedded on websites or shared as links.

Several features support data communication. Over thirty chart types, including maps and tables, handle different kinds of data, and live data connections update visuals when the source changes. Teams can collaborate on projects, keep brand templates, and publish with analytics. Downloads include images and PDFs, and AI features help generate visuals and suggest ways to present data.

item.title: Kaedim
item.description:
Kaedim addresses a slow stage in game and digital content production: turning concept art into 3D assets. You upload an image of a character, prop, or environment piece, and Kaedim produces a 3D model that matches it. The aim is to give artists a solid starting point they can refine, which cuts down the days of modeling work needed for each asset.

The service has been known for mixing machine learning with human review. Models go through checks by 3D artists who clean up errors before they are delivered, which improves reliability compared with fully automatic generators, but may slow turnaround. Output can be downloaded in common formats and used in engines like Unity and Unreal or imported into Blender and Maya for editing. Teams use it for game props, virtual production, and prototyping product ideas.

item.title: Langflow
item.description:
Langflow makes it possible to design an AI application by connecting blocks on a canvas. Components represent language models, prompts, memory, document loaders, vector stores, and tools, and you wire them together to define how data flows. An integrated playground lets you chat with the flow, inspect each step, and adjust it, which is useful for experimenting with retrieval and agent behavior without writing a full application.

Flows can be exported and run as API endpoints or embedded in apps, and you can write custom components in Python when the built-in ones are not enough. It works with many model providers and vector databases, and supports multi-agent setups and Model Context Protocol servers. Teams use it for prototypes, internal assistants, and RAG pipelines before moving to code.

item.title: Later
item.description:
Later started as a way to plan Instagram feeds visually. Users drag photos and videos onto a calendar, see how the grid will look, write captions, and schedule posts to go out automatically. It has since expanded to other networks, including TikTok, Pinterest, LinkedIn, Facebook, and X, with tools to manage a content library, collaborate with teammates, and track results.

Other features support social growth. A link-in-bio page lets creators send followers to multiple destinations, analytics show which posts perform best and when audiences are most active, and AI helps write captions, suggest hashtags, and repurpose content. The company also owns an influencer marketing platform, which helps brands find creators and manage campaigns.

item.title: Lucidchart AI
item.description:
Lucidchart is a mature online diagramming tool from Lucid Software. Users create flowcharts, process maps, org charts, wireframes, network diagrams, and technical drawings with a large library of shapes and templates, and collaborate in real time with comments and version history. Because it runs in the browser and integrates with the tools that teams already use, it’s popular in business and IT.

Several features go beyond drawing. Data linking can generate org charts or network diagrams from spreadsheets and cloud accounts, so diagrams stay current, and a presentation mode turns diagrams into slides. AI features generate diagrams from a text description, suggest improvements, and summarize complex drawings. Lucidchart is part of the Lucid suite, which also includes Lucidspark for whiteboarding and Lucidscale for cloud diagrams.

item.title: Ludo.ai
item.description:
Ludo.ai aims to speed up the early stages of game development. Designers can brainstorm game concepts and mechanics, get suggestions based on trends in app stores, and generate descriptions and feature lists. A market research tool analyzes top-performing games to show what genres and themes are popular, which helps indie studios and publishers decide what to build.

The platform includes asset generation. It can produce concept art and character designs, sprites and sprite sheets, short animations, UI elements, and sound effects and music from prompts, and convert images into basic 3D models in some plans. Outputs are intended for prototypes and mockups to test ideas quickly, and can be exported for use in engines like Unity.

item.title: Mage.space
item.description:
Mage.space gives people a simple front end for open-source image models. You choose from a catalog of checkpoints, write a prompt, adjust settings like style, size, and number of images, and generate. It supports image-to-image transformations, inpainting, and control features that guide composition, and results can be upscaled. Because it hosts the models, users do not need a powerful computer or a local installation.

The platform appeals to people who want flexibility in styles, from realistic photos to anime and fantasy art, and who want to experiment with community-trained models. It has a gallery of public creations, and a text-to-video tool has been added to some plans. Content rules are looser than on some mainstream services, though it still prohibits illegal material.

item.title: Make
item.description: Make, formerly called Integromat, lets you automate work between apps by drawing it. You place modules on a canvas for each app, such as Gmail, Google Sheets, Slack, or a CRM, and connect them with lines that show how data flows. You can add routers that split the flow into branches, filters that decide which items continue, iterators that handle lists, and functions that change data on the way. This visual layout makes complicated logic easier to follow than a long linear list of steps.

item.title: Masterpiece Studio
item.description:
Masterpiece Studio began with virtual reality tools for sculpting, painting, and animating in 3D, making 3D creation more intuitive for artists. It later moved toward generative AI, with Masterpiece X, which generates 3D models from text or images. Users describe an object, and the system produces a mesh with textures that can be refined or used as a starting point for game assets, virtual worlds, and prototypes.

The aim is to make output useful in production. Generated models can be downloaded in common formats and used in game engines such as Unity and Unreal, or opened in Blender and other tools for editing. Additional features help with rigging and animation, so characters can be posed and moved without a complex setup. A no-code approach targets creators who do not have a modeling background, including developers and designers who need many assets.

item.title: Meta AI
item.description: Meta AI is the assistant that Meta put where its users already are. In WhatsApp, Instagram, Messenger, and Facebook, you can mention it in a chat or open it from the search bar to ask a question, get recommendations, or generate an image. There is also a standalone app and website with fuller features, including natural voice conversations, image creation and editing, and a feed where people share what they have made.

item.title: Midjourney
item.description: Midjourney is one of the most popular image generators, valued for its distinctive aesthetic. You describe an image, and it returns variations that tend to look polished and painterly, with strong composition and lighting. It began on Discord, where users type commands in a shared channel, and now offers a web interface with an image editor, personal galleries, and organization tools. It’s widely used by illustrators, designers, concept artists, and marketers.

item.title: Miro AI
item.description:
Miro provides an infinite shared canvas where teams place sticky notes, diagrams, documents, and images, and work together live or asynchronously. It’s used for brainstorming, retrospectives, user journey maps, roadmaps, and workshops, particularly for distributed teams. A large library of templates, integrations with tools such as Jira, Slack, and Google Drive, and facilitation features like timers and voting make it versatile.

AI features speed up creation and synthesis. Users can generate diagrams, flowcharts, and mind maps from a prompt, summarize and cluster hundreds of sticky notes into themes, and turn a board into a document or a prototype. Sidekicks are AI helpers with specific roles, such as a product manager or a retrospective facilitator, that give feedback and suggestions on the board. Flows connect several AI steps for repeatable processes.

item.title: Missinglettr
item.description:
Missinglettr automates a task many content creators neglect: promoting their articles over time. You connect your blog or paste a link, and the tool analyzes the post to pull out quotes, statistics, and highlights. It then generates a series of social posts, with images, scheduled across weeks and months, so a single article continues to attract visitors long after it’s published.

Other features round out the platform. A curation tool suggests relevant content from other sources to share, a social media scheduler handles regular posting, and analytics show engagement. Collaboration features allow agencies and teams to manage several brands. AI helps with writing captions and variations, and automated hashtag suggestions save time.

item.title: Monday.com
item.description:
Monday.com organizes work in colorful boards that resemble spreadsheets. Teams track projects, sales pipelines, marketing campaigns, and operations with columns for status, owners, dates, and more, and view the same data as a timeline, calendar, or chart. No-code automations handle routine updates and notifications.

The platform has expanded into products for sales CRM, service desks, and software development, built on the same foundation. AI assistants create boards from a description, summarize items and updates, write content, and extract information, and agents can take on tasks within workflows.

item.title: Neural.love
item.description:
Neural.love combines creation and repair tools in one web app. The generator creates images from text prompts with a choice of models and styles, while the enhancement tools improve existing pictures. Upscaling increases resolution, denoising cleans grainy photos, and restoration repairs scratches and faded color on old family pictures. Face enhancement can sharpen portraits, and colorization adds color to black-and-white images.

The platform is practical for photographers, genealogists, designers, and anyone with old or low-quality images. Users upload a file, choose the effect, and download the result, with credits consumed by each operation. An API lets developers add enhancement features to their own apps, and batch options handle many images. Generated images can be used in marketing and design, subject to the terms for each plan.

item.title: Obsidian
item.description: Obsidian treats notes as local files. Everything you write is a Markdown document in a folder on your computer, so you own the data and can open it with any other editor. You connect notes with links, and the app shows backlinks and a graph view of how ideas relate. People use it for personal knowledge management, research, writing, journaling, and project notes, and many build large networks of thousands of linked notes over years.

item.title: OpenRead
item.description:
OpenRead is built for people who read a lot of research. After you import a paper, an AI assistant can answer questions about it, explain terms, summarize sections, and pull out items like methods, results, and limitations. A structured summary view lays out the main points in a consistent format, which helps when scanning many papers for a review.

The platform extends beyond a single paper. It helps search the literature, organize papers into collections, take notes alongside the text, and generate outlines or review drafts from selected sources. Support for multiple languages makes it useful for researchers who read in a second language, and translation features help with papers published in other languages.

item.title: Paige.AI
item.description:
Paige works on a part of medicine where AI could make a real difference: pathology, in which specialists examine tissue slides to diagnose cancer. Slides are scanned into very large digital images, and Paige’s algorithms analyze them, flagging areas that look suspicious and helping pathologists find cancer more efficiently and consistently. Its prostate cancer detection software was the first AI pathology tool to receive FDA clearance.

The company grew out of a collaboration with Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center and built a large collection of digitized slides paired with clinical and molecular data. It developed foundation models trained on millions of slides to support a broad range of cancer analysis tasks, and offers a platform for laboratories to deploy AI tools alongside digital pathology systems.

item.title: Paperspace
item.description:
Paperspace rents GPU computing by the hour. Users launch virtual machines with GPUs for training models, running experiments, or heavy graphics, and connect remotely. Gradient adds managed Jupyter notebooks and workflows that make it easy to start without setting up servers.

DigitalOcean acquired Paperspace and has been integrating it with its cloud offerings, aiming to give developers and small teams access to GPUs with simple pricing. Students and independent researchers have long used it for coursework and experiments.

item.title: Pattern89
item.description:
Pattern89 set out to bring data to creative decisions. Advertisers produce many images and videos but often cannot tell which elements drive results. The platform analyzed an advertiser’s past ads and performance data, tagging the visual and text elements in each, such as colors, faces, products, and calls to action, and learned which combinations worked for a given audience and channel.

With that knowledge, it could score new creative before launch and suggest changes, and recommend which assets to prioritize. Marketers used it to reduce wasted spend on ads that were unlikely to work, and to give designers concrete guidance. Integrations with social ad platforms pulled in performance data.

item.title: Perplexity Pages
item.description:
Pages is a publishing layer on top of Perplexity’s research. After you explore a topic with the assistant, you can convert the thread into a structured page with headings, summaries, and citations to the sources it used. It organizes the material in the way a short article or study guide would be written, instead of leaving you with a conversation log.

You control the result. Sections can be rewritten, reordered, or removed, images can be added, and the page can be published with a shareable link or kept private. Educators use Pages to create study guides, students for report drafts, and professionals for quick explainers on topics they research often. Because the citations travel with the content, readers can check where claims came from.

item.title: Picsart AI
item.description:
Picsart began as a mobile photo editor and grew into a broad creative suite. Users edit photos with filters, collages, stickers, and text, make videos, and design social posts from templates. A community lets people share and remix content, which helped it spread among younger creators and small businesses.

AI is now central. Tools generate images from prompts, remove backgrounds and objects, expand pictures, replace elements, enhance and upscale photos, and create stylized avatars. Text-to-video and animation tools turn ideas into clips, and an AI writer helps with captions. Picsart also provides APIs and plugins so other platforms can use its image tools, and teams can use brand kits and shared workspaces.

item.title: Pika Labs
item.description: Pika grew popular by making AI video fun and easy for people with no editing experience. You type a prompt or upload an image, and it generates a short clip in a few moments. Its signature features are effects that change objects in playful ways, such as melting, squishing, inflating, or turning something into cake, which spread quickly across social media. The interface is simple and mobile-friendly, which suited creators who make clips for TikTok and Instagram.

item.title: Pika Labs
item.description:
Pika makes short video easy. A user types a prompt, uploads an image, or provides a clip, and Pika generates or modifies footage. It is known for playful effects, like making objects melt or inflate, as well as realistic motion and camera control.

Creators use it for social posts, ads, and concept work. Features include editing parts of a video, extending clips, adding sound, and lip sync. The platform has expanded to support multiple underlying models and mobile apps.

item.title: Piktochart
item.description: Piktochart is aimed at people who need to present information visually but are not designers. You choose a template for an infographic, report, presentation, or poster, edit the text and images, and add charts and maps that you can link to data. Visual blocks, icons, illustrations, and a library of graphics make it quick to produce clean results, and the tool exports to image and PDF formats or shares online.

item.title: Pixelcut
item.description:
Pixelcut focuses on product images. A seller photographs an item, removes the background in one tap, and places the product on a clean or styled backdrop. AI can generate scenes that suit a product, add shadows, and upscale low-resolution pictures.

Batch tools process many images, and templates help create ads, social posts, and listing graphics. The mobile app is popular with small sellers who shoot products with a phone.

Pixelcut has a free tier and paid plans. AI-generated scenes should still show the product accurately to avoid returns. Alternatives include Photoroom, Canva, Pebblely, Remove.bg, and Adobe Express. Pixelcut suits small online sellers.

item.title: Planet Labs
item.description: Planet Labs built its business on frequency. Rather than a few large satellites, it operates a large number of small ones, so it can photograph almost every part of the land surface regularly. That consistency allows users to watch change over time: crops growing, forests being cleared, ice melting, construction progressing, or ships moving. The imagery has a lower resolution than the sharpest commercial satellites but far greater frequency, and some higher-resolution satellites supplement it.

item.title: Planner 5D
item.description:
Planner 5D lets anyone design interiors. A user draws walls and rooms, adds furniture from a large catalog, and views the result in 3D from any angle or as a realistic render. It is aimed at homeowners and hobbyists planning remodels, with simple controls.

AI features generate design suggestions from a room photo, restyle spaces, and build floor plans from sketches. A community gallery provides projects to copy and adapt. Mobile and web apps share projects.

item.title: Plasmic
item.description:
Plasmic connects visual design with real code. Developers register their React components in Plasmic, and designers and marketers can then drag those components onto a canvas, adjust styling and content, and publish pages without waiting for a code release. Alternatively, Plasmic can build entire pages and sites itself, and its output integrates with frameworks like Next.js, Gatsby, and plain React.

Features help teams collaborate. A CMS stores content, responsive design controls handle layouts across devices, and the editor includes interactions, animations, and data bindings. Teams can use it to build landing pages, marketing sites, and web apps, while developers stay in control of the underlying components. Code can be exported or used with a runtime, which reduces lock-in.

item.title: Playground AI
item.description:
Playground started as a place to experiment with image models in a friendly interface. You enter a prompt, choose a model and style, and generate images, then refine them in a canvas that lets you edit parts of a picture, combine elements, and iterate. It was positioned as a flexible tool for artists, designers, and marketers, with a free daily allowance that made it popular for experimentation.

The company has also developed its own image models, which it has promoted for following prompts closely and rendering text, along with tools for creating logos, posters, and social graphics. Image-to-image, upscaling, and editing by instruction help refine results. Users can browse a community feed to see what others are making and borrow ideas.

item.title: Power BI
item.description: Power BI turns raw data into visual reports. You connect to sources such as Excel files, SQL databases, cloud services, and Microsoft Fabric, shape the data, define relationships and calculations, and build dashboards with charts, maps, and slicers. Reports can be published to the Power BI service, shared with colleagues, refreshed on a schedule, and embedded in other applications. Because it fits neatly with Excel, Teams, SharePoint, and Azure, it is the default BI tool for many Microsoft-centered companies.

item.title: Real-ESRGAN
item.description:
Real-ESRGAN takes a small, blurry, or compressed image and produces a larger, cleaner version. It was trained on synthetic damage that imitates real-world degradation, such as blur, noise, and compression artifacts, so it handles messy sources better than older upscalers that assumed clean images. The results often look natural, with sharper edges and textures, although the model adds plausible detail instead of recovering what was truly there.

The project provides several models, including one for general photos and one for anime and illustrations, plus tools for video that process frames. Portable builds run on Windows, macOS, and Linux using Vulkan, so no complicated setup or Nvidia GPU is needed, and Python code lets developers integrate it. It is often paired with GFPGAN for face restoration. Many commercial upscaling tools and apps use Real-ESRGAN or models derived from it.

item.title: ResearchRabbit
item.description:
ResearchRabbit helps researchers find papers they would not discover through keyword search. You add a few papers to a collection, and the tool suggests related earlier work, later work that cites them, and papers by connected authors, showing the connections in visual graphs. As you add more papers, recommendations get more specific, which makes it behave like a recommendation engine for research.

Collections keep projects organized, and alerts notify you when new papers match your interests. You can see networks of authors, explore how a field evolved, and export references to managers like Zotero. It is popular with students and academics who are starting a literature review or entering a new topic, and who want something more exploratory than a search box.

item.title: Roboflow
item.description:
Roboflow helps teams build computer vision applications without starting from scratch. You upload images or video, label objects with AI-assisted annotation tools, and Roboflow handles formatting, augmentation, and splitting data into training sets. It then trains or fine-tunes models such as YOLO and other popular architectures, and shows performance metrics so you can see where the model fails and what data to add.

Deployment is a main focus. Models can run through a hosted API, on your own servers, or at the edge on devices such as NVIDIA Jetson or a mobile phone. Workflows let you chain models with logic and actions, for example detecting a defect, counting items, and sending an alert to a system. Roboflow Universe is a public collection of datasets and pretrained models shared by the community, which gives a fast start for common tasks.

item.title: Runway
item.description:
Runway builds tools for creative professionals. Its generative video models create clips from text or images, and a suite of editing tools handles tasks like removing backgrounds, changing motion, extending shots, and applying styles. Everything runs in the browser.

The company began with accessible video editing and became a leader in generative video, working with artists and studios. Newer models offer longer clips, better consistency, and controls for camera and motion, and the platform includes workflows for combining generation with traditional editing.

item.title: Runway
item.description: Runway is one of the original AI video companies, and it built its tools with filmmakers and artists in mind. The core of the product is its Gen video models, which create short clips from a text prompt, a still image, or both. Reference images help keep a character or setting consistent from one shot to the next, which is the hard part of making anything longer than a single clip. The company started as a set of browser-based editing tools, and some of that remains, such as background removal, motion tracking, and inpainting.

item.title: Runway Gen-3
item.description:
Gen-3 Alpha improved on earlier versions with finer detail, better handling of motion, and more consistent results across frames. Users could generate clips of several seconds from a prompt, an image, or both, with controls for camera movement and style.

It was trained on both images and video, aiming to understand how things move, and supported features such as image-to-video and video-to-video. Filmmakers and agencies used it for concept work, ads, and visual effects experiments.

item.title: Scenario
item.description:
Scenario is built around consistency, which is the main challenge of using generative AI in game production. A studio uploads examples of its art, and Scenario trains a custom model that learns the style, so the characters, props, and environments it generates look like they belong in the same game. Artists can use it to create concepts, variations, and finished assets faster.

The platform covers more than still images. It can generate sprites, textures, icons, and UI elements, create variations of existing pieces, convert images into 3D models, and offers workflows for upscaling and cleaning outputs. An API and plugins connect it to game engines and pipelines, and team features support collaboration and asset management. The focus is on production use by studios and indie developers.

item.title: SeaArt
item.description: SeaArt gives users a rich set of image generation tools in a friendly interface. You write a prompt, choose among many models and styles, and generate images, with options such as ControlNet to guide pose or composition and LoRA models to apply particular styles or characters. A library of community-shared models, workflows, and characters lets users build on others’ work, and a node-based workflow editor offers more advanced control for those who want it.

item.title: SimilarWeb
item.description:
Similarweb lets you look at the performance of sites you do not own. Enter a domain, and it shows estimated monthly visits, traffic sources such as search, social, and direct, top keywords, referring sites, audience demographics, and engagement metrics like time on site. Data comes from a mix of panels, partnerships, and public sources, modeled to produce estimates. This helps in benchmarking competitors and finding growth opportunities.

The platform covers more than websites. It tracks app usage and downloads, advertising, and market segments, and ranks sites within categories. Recent additions include tracking how brands and sites are cited and visited through AI chatbots, reflecting the way people increasingly use AI assistants instead of search. Investors use the data to spot trends in company performance before financial reports, and sales teams use it to find leads.

item.title: SketchUp
item.description: SketchUp is known for being easy to learn. Its core idea is pushing and pulling flat shapes into 3D forms, which makes it quick to sketch a building, a room, or a piece of furniture. Architects use it for early design, interior designers for layouts, and construction and woodworking professionals for planning and shop drawings. The 3D Warehouse offers a huge library of free models of furniture, fixtures, and building components.

item.title: Socratic by Google
item.description:
Socratic began as a startup and was acquired by Google, which relaunched it as a free app for students. A learner took a photo of a homework problem, and the app identified the concept and pointed to videos, explanations, and step-by-step guidance from across the web instead of just giving an answer.

It covered subjects such as math, science, and literature, and used machine learning to match questions to educational content. The goal was to help students understand a topic, not only to produce a solution.

item.title: Stability AI
item.description:
Stability AI helped start the open-source image generation boom with Stable Diffusion, a model anyone could download, run, and modify. The release spurred a huge community of tools, fine-tunes, and applications, and changed expectations about access to generative models.

The company has since released a family of models, including newer image generators, Stable Video Diffusion, Stable Audio for music and sound, and 3D tools. It sells API access and commercial licenses, and partners with enterprises, and with media and entertainment companies.

item.title: Stable Video Diffusion
item.description:
Stable Video Diffusion extends the Stable Diffusion approach to motion. A user supplies a still image, and the model generates a few seconds of video that animates the scene. It was released with open weights, so researchers and hobbyists could run and adapt it.

Many later tools and workflows built on it, adding controls, longer clips, and fine-tunes. It helped prove that open video models were feasible, though newer models from other labs have surpassed it in length and quality.

item.title: StarryAI
item.description:
StarryAI brought AI art generation to phones. In the app, you enter a text prompt, pick an art style or model, and receive images within a minute or so. Styles range from fantasy and anime to realism and abstract, and you can use an image as a starting point for variations. It’s aimed at hobbyists and creators who want art for wallpapers, profile pictures, book covers, or game concepts.

Features support experimentation. You can control aspect ratio, choose among models, and upscale results, and a gallery shows creations from other users for inspiration. Different pricing tiers offer more credits and faster generation, and the terms for commercial use vary by plan, with ownership of outputs depending on the subscription.

item.title: Tableau
item.description:
Tableau is known for making data exploration feel visual and quick. Analysts connect to databases, spreadsheets, and cloud data warehouses, then drag fields onto a canvas to build charts, maps, and dashboards without writing code. It handles large data volumes well, and its interactivity lets viewers filter, drill down, and compare in ways static reports cannot. It is widely used in finance, healthcare, retail, government, and education.

Salesforce owns Tableau and has built AI into it. Tableau Pulse sends personalized, plain-language insights about key metrics to the people who care about them, and flags unusual changes without anyone opening a dashboard. Tableau Agent helps users build visualizations and analyze data by chatting with the tool. Tableau Prep cleans and combines data, and the platform integrates with Salesforce data and its Data Cloud.

item.title: Tome
item.description:
Tome became a popular early example of generative AI for presentations. A user described a topic, and Tome produced a complete, designed narrative with text, images, and layout, which could be edited in a flexible, canvas-like format. It was positioned as a more modern, storytelling-focused alternative to PowerPoint, and gained millions of users, with attention from students, founders, and professionals.

The company later decided to retire the presentation product and pivot to something different, a sales-focused application. Users were given a period to export their work before the service closed. The pivot reflected a challenge facing many AI tools: general features are quickly matched by larger products, and a standalone app needs a defensible niche.

item.title: Topaz Photo AI
item.description:
Topaz Photo AI aims to fix the technical flaws in photos with little effort. When you open an image, it analyzes the content and suggests corrections, using models for noise reduction, sharpening, and increasing resolution. It handles problems like grainy high-ISO shots, soft focus, and motion blur, and can enlarge photos while adding believable detail. Many wildlife, sports, and event photographers use it to rescue difficult images.

The tool also offers face recovery, light adjustment, color balance, and a way to apply different adjustments to selected subjects. It can be run as a standalone application, as an external editor from Lightroom, or as a plugin for Photoshop, and processes batches of images. Models run locally on your computer and benefit from a good graphics card.

item.title: Vectorizer.ai
item.description:
Vectorizer.ai converts bitmap images into vectors, which are scalable files used for logos, print, and cutting machines. Upload a low-resolution logo or illustration, and the service traces the shapes into paths and fills, returning an SVG, EPS, PDF, or DXF that can be resized without losing sharpness. The AI approach produces cleaner curves and fewer stray points than older tracing tools, with controls to adjust the level of detail.

Designers use it to recover logos from low-quality files, sign makers and crafters use it to prepare artwork for vinyl cutters and laser engravers, and developers add it to workflows through an API. It handles flat-color artwork best, such as logos and icons, and it works less well on photographs, which turn into complex tracings with many shapes. A preview lets you see the result before paying.

item.title: Venice AI
item.description: Venice AI builds its pitch around privacy and freedom of use. The company states it does not log or store conversations on its servers, and that chats are kept in the user’s browser, which appeals to people uneasy about their prompts being retained or used for training. It runs open-source models, so users can pick from several language models and an image generator, and the platform applies fewer content restrictions than many mainstream services.

item.title: Venngage
item.description:
Venngage targets people who need to communicate information visually. Users start from thousands of templates for infographics, reports, flyers, presentations, and social graphics, replace the content, and customize colors, icons, and charts. Data can be imported to generate charts, and the tool includes maps and diagrams for explaining processes and comparisons.

It differentiates itself with business features. Brand kits apply logos, fonts, and colors automatically, team workspaces allow collaboration and approvals, and an accessibility checker flags color contrast and other issues. AI tools generate infographic designs from text, write copy, and suggest improvements, and designs can be exported or shared with analytics.

item.title: Visme AI
item.description:
Visme is aimed at people who need to present information visually without design skills. It offers a drag-and-drop editor with thousands of templates for presentations, infographics, reports, charts, social media posts, and documents. Data widgets create charts and graphs from spreadsheets, and interactive elements such as links and animations can be added. Brand kits keep colors, fonts, and logos consistent across a team.

AI features speed up creation. An AI designer can generate a presentation or document from a prompt, write and rewrite text, create images, and suggest layouts. Teams can collaborate in real time with comments and workflows, and content can be exported as PDF, PowerPoint, or HTML, or shared by link with analytics. Visme is often used by marketers, educators, consultants, and communications teams.

item.title: Vue.ai
item.description:
Vue.ai is built for retailers with large catalogs. Computer vision reads product images and assigns attributes such as color, pattern, neckline, fabric, and occasion, which saves teams from tagging thousands of items by hand. Those tags feed search, filters, and merchandising, so shoppers find items that match what they want.

The same data drives the customer-facing side. Recommendation engines suggest items based on browsing and purchase behavior, visual search lets shoppers upload a photo to find similar products, and styling tools suggest outfits that go together. Merchandisers can also see how products perform and adjust collections and layouts.

item.title: Whimsical AI
item.description:
Whimsical puts several lightweight visual tools in one place. You can draw flowcharts and sequence diagrams, sketch low-fidelity wireframes, brainstorm on mind maps, write docs, and arrange sticky notes on a board. The tools are designed around speed, with keyboard shortcuts, snapping, and a clean look that makes rough thinking easy to share.

AI features reduce the setup. Describe a process and Whimsical can draft a flowchart, turn a topic into a mind map, or produce a first-pass wireframe, which you then edit by hand. Teams use it for planning, product specs, and explaining systems, and sharing is simple with links, comments, and embeds in tools like Notion and Confluence.

item.title: Wix ADI
item.description:
Wix ADI, short for Artificial Design Intelligence, was an early attempt at automatic site building. A user answered questions about their business and style, and ADI generated a layout with text, images, and a structure suited to the industry. It let people with no design skills get a website online in minutes, long before generative AI was common.

ADI sites had limits. They used a simpler editor than the main Wix Editor, which made it hard to customize them or to add advanced features. Wix has since retired the product: ADI sites are no longer supported and existing ones were moved into the standard Wix Editor, so owners can keep editing them there.

item.title: Alpha3D
item.description: Alpha3D addresses a bottleneck in 3D content: modeling each object by hand is slow and expensive. Instead, you upload a photo of a product or describe an object in text, and the platform generates a 3D model, typically within minutes. The models can be downloaded in common formats such as GLB for use in game engines, web viewers, and AR experiences. The company positions it for retail, gaming, and virtual try-on.

item.title: Botpress
item.description: Botpress started as an open-source tool for building chatbots with visual flows, and it grew into a platform around large language models. Developers and technical teams build agents that talk with customers on websites and messaging channels, connect to knowledge bases, and call APIs to do things like check an order or update an account. A visual builder and code options sit side by side, so non-engineers can adjust conversations while developers handle integrations.

item.title: Cloudflare Workers AI
item.description:
Workers AI brings model inference close to users. A developer writes a Cloudflare Worker, calls a model through a binding or REST API, and Cloudflare runs it on GPUs in its data centers around the world. There are no servers to manage, and the platform scales automatically.

The catalog includes open models for chat and text generation, embeddings, image generation, speech recognition, translation, and classification. Developers combine it with other Cloudflare products, such as Vectorize for vector search, D1 for databases, R2 for storage, and AI Gateway for monitoring, to build full applications at the edge.

item.title: Evidently AI
item.description:
Evidently helps teams know whether their models are working. The open-source library computes metrics and produces interactive reports on data drift, data quality, model accuracy, and, for language model applications, aspects such as relevance and safety. It can run in notebooks, in pipelines, or as a monitoring service.

For LLM work, Evidently supports evaluations with test sets, automated judges, and tracing, so teams can compare prompt versions and catch regressions. A hosted platform adds dashboards, alerting, and collaboration, and the project has a large community and educational material on ML observability.

item.title: Fal.ai
item.description:
fal.ai gives developers a fast way to use generative media models without managing GPUs. A team calls an API for models that produce images, video, audio, and 3D assets, and fal handles the infrastructure, scaling, and optimization. Its speed is the main pitch, which matters for apps where users wait on each generation.

The catalog includes popular open models and models from partners, and the platform is used by consumer apps, design tools, and companies that add generation features to their products. Developers can also deploy their own models and fine-tunes on its serverless compute, and use dedicated GPUs for steady workloads.

item.title: Hedra
item.description:
Hedra animates faces. A user supplies a still image, which can be a photo, illustration, or generated character, and an audio track or script, and Hedra produces a video of the character speaking with matching lip movement and expression. The results are known for emotive performances.

Uses include short films, explainer videos, social content with characters, and marketing. Text to speech and voice options make it possible to start from only a script, and longer and higher resolution outputs are available on paid plans. The platform has expanded into broader video generation features.

item.title: Kaiber
item.description:
Kaiber is known for stylized, artistic video. A user supplies a prompt, an image, or a video clip, chooses a style, and the platform generates moving footage in that look. Audio reactivity lets visuals respond to a music track, which made it a favorite for music videos and live visuals.

The platform has grown into a broader creative studio with a canvas for combining generated images and video and with access to several underlying models. Artists use it to experiment with motion and aesthetics rather than realistic footage, and it has been featured in music video projects.

item.title: Lexica
item.description:
Lexica began as a searchable archive of AI-generated images with the prompts that created them. Browsing the archive helped people learn how wording affects results, and copy ideas for their own generations. That made it a popular learning resource in the early days of image generators.

The platform added its own image generation models and an editor, so users can create images, refine them, and organize collections. It offers different model options and tools for art, product shots, and concepts. The community library remains a source of inspiration.

item.title: Lummi
item.description:
Lummi collects AI-generated pictures in a searchable library, organized by category and style. Users browse or search for backgrounds, textures, scenes, and illustrations, then download them for use in websites, presentations, and campaigns. The pitch is variety and a modern look compared with familiar stock photography.

The platform includes generation tools that let users create images from prompts and adjust them, along with options for editing. It is popular with designers who want unusual or abstract visuals and do not want to prompt from scratch.

item.title: Magnific AI
item.description:
Magnific AI takes a low-resolution image and produces a larger version with added, invented detail. Users control how much creative freedom the AI takes with settings such as creativity and resemblance, and can add a prompt describing what the detail should look like. This makes it different from conventional upscalers.

Artists use it to polish AI-generated images and to turn rough concept art into detailed illustrations. Designers use it to prepare images for large formats. The company was acquired by Freepik, and the technology is available through Magnific’s own site and Freepik’s tools.

item.title: Marqo
item.description:
Marqo handles vector search end to end. A developer sends documents or images to Marqo, and it generates embeddings with a chosen model, stores them, and serves similarity queries, so there is no separate pipeline for embedding and indexing. Queries can combine text and images, which suits product search.

The company has focused on e-commerce relevance, offering models trained for product search and tools to improve ranking with feedback from user behavior. It runs as a self-hosted open-source service or as a managed cloud.

item.title: Milvus
item.description:
Milvus is built for scale. It stores high-dimensional vectors, which represent text, images, or other data, and finds the nearest neighbors quickly even among billions of items. It supports different index types, filtering with metadata, and hybrid search that combines vectors and keywords.

The architecture separates storage and compute so it can run across a cluster, and there are lighter modes for development. It is part of the Linux Foundation’s AI & Data group, and Zilliz offers a managed cloud service with additional features.

item.title: Morph Studio
item.description:
Morph Studio lets users create video through prompts and images. It offers a storyboard interface, where a creator plans shots, generates each, and assembles them into a sequence, which suits narrative content more than single clips. Different models and styles are available.

Creators use it for short films, ads, music videos, and social content. The workflow supports iteration: regenerate a shot, adjust the prompt, and compare results. Community features let users share work and learn techniques.

item.title: PathAI
item.description:
PathAI works on digital pathology. Pathologists traditionally examine tissue slides under a microscope. With scanned slides, algorithms can highlight regions of interest, count cells, and measure biomarkers, which helps make reads more consistent. PathAI builds these tools and a platform for viewing and managing slides.

The company also supports pharmaceutical research. Its models analyze tissue from clinical trials to measure disease features and treatment responses, and it operates a laboratory service. The goal is to reduce variability and speed drug development.

item.title: Pory
item.description:
Pory turns spreadsheets and databases into websites. A user connects an Airtable base or Google Sheet, designs pages and layouts with a visual editor, and publishes a directory, portal, or dashboard. Logins and permissions control who sees what.

It is popular for member directories, job boards, simple CRMs, and client portals. Because the data stays in the source, updating the spreadsheet updates the site.

Pory has a free tier and paid plans. Complex logic is limited compared with full app builders. Alternatives include Softr, Glide, Stacker, Noloco, and Bubble. Pory suits non-developers building front ends on Airtable or Sheets.

item.title: Recraft
item.description:
Recraft is aimed at designers. Besides raster images, it can produce true vector graphics, such as logos, icons, and illustrations, that remain sharp at any size and can be edited in design software. Style controls keep outputs consistent across a project.

Brand features let a team upload colors, fonts, and example images so generations follow a style. The model handles text in images well, which helps with posters and mockups. Editing tools allow changing parts of an image, removing backgrounds, and upscaling.

item.title: Reka AI
item.description:
Reka is a research lab and company founded by researchers from DeepMind, Google, and Meta. It trains models from scratch that take mixed inputs, so a user can ask questions about a video or combine audio and text. The Flash and Edge models are smaller and faster, and Core is the largest.

Products built on the models include tools for research tasks that search and reason over the web, and for analyzing video. Developers use the API, and the company has released some models openly. Efficiency is a recurring theme in its work.

item.title: Riffusion
item.description:
Riffusion started as a research demo that generated music clips by running Stable Diffusion on spectrogram images, an early sign that diffusion models could make audio. It grew into a platform where users type a prompt and get a song with vocals, and into a chat-like agent that helps produce tracks.

The brand changed to Producer.ai, and reports say it has since moved under Google’s music efforts, so product names and features may keep changing. Users should check the current site and how their saved songs and rights are handled through any transition.

item.title: Rodin
item.description:
Rodin creates 3D assets from simple inputs. A user types a description or uploads an image, and the system produces a textured 3D model that can be exported to common formats. It also offers options for controlling geometry and materials.

The output can serve as a starting point for games, animation, product visualization, and augmented reality. Quality has improved quickly in this field, but generated meshes often need cleanup of topology and textures before production use.

item.title: RoomGPT
item.description:
RoomGPT lets people visualize a space in new styles. A user uploads a photo of a living room or bedroom, chooses a theme such as modern, minimalist, or tropical, and the AI generates redesigned images that keep the room’s structure while changing furniture and decor.

Homeowners use it for inspiration before shopping or renovating, and some real estate agents use it for staging ideas. Results show style direction but do not match real products or exact dimensions.

item.title: Stablecog
item.description:
Stablecog offers image generation without the setup of running a model locally. Users enter a prompt, choose a model and settings, and receive images in seconds. The code is open, and the project is run as a community-minded service.

It appeals to hobbyists who want to try Stable Diffusion and its variants and to developers who want a reference for building their own interface. Free credits are available, with paid options for more use.

item.title: Tensor.Art
item.description:
Tensor.Art lets people create images without owning a GPU. They choose from a library of models and LoRAs trained by the community, type a prompt, and generate images, often in styles from anime to realism. Workflows can be remixed, and results shared in a gallery.

The platform supports training custom models, running ComfyUI-based workflows, and generating video, and it has a credit system for heavy use. It appeals to hobbyists and artists who want variety.

item.title: Vellum
item.description:
Vellum supports teams building AI features for production. Developers and product managers write and compare prompts across models, build workflows that chain steps, and run evaluations against test sets before releasing changes.

Deployment and monitoring tools track versions, costs, and quality, and let teams update prompts without redeploying code. A visual builder and SDK suit both technical and non-technical members.

Vellum has a free tier and paid plans. Alternatives include Langfuse, LangSmith, Braintrust, PromptLayer, and Humanloop, which has shut down. Vellum suits product teams shipping LLM features.

item.title: Vidu
item.description:
Vidu turns prompts into short videos. A user writes a description or supplies reference images, and the platform generates a clip. Features include reference-to-video, which keeps a character or object consistent across shots, and templates for effects that are popular in social content.

The company is one of several Chinese labs competing in video generation, alongside Kling, MiniMax, and others, and its models have gained attention for motion quality and speed. Creators use it for short films, ads, and animation tests.

item.title: Voiceflow
item.description:
Voiceflow lets teams design conversational agents together. On a visual canvas, designers and developers map out how an agent should respond, add steps that call language models, search knowledge bases, run logic, and connect to APIs and tools. Non-engineers can shape conversations while developers handle integrations, which makes it practical for cross-functional teams in customer support, sales, and operations.

The platform handles the whole lifecycle. You can add a knowledge base of company content so the agent answers from it, test the agent in a built-in environment, and deploy it to a website, messaging channels, phone lines, or via API. Analytics and transcripts show how conversations go, and versioning and collaboration features support teamwork. Voiceflow works with a choice of language models.

item.title: AI Aware
item.description:
AI Aware presents itself as a tool for checking whether content was written or generated by AI. Users upload a document or paste text, and the service returns an estimate of how likely it is to be machine-generated, along with detail on which parts raised the score. The idea is to give educators, publishers, and businesses a quick way to screen material.

Detection of AI-generated content is a difficult problem. Detectors rely on statistical patterns that can also appear in human writing, especially in formal or non-native text, and they can be fooled by editing or paraphrasing. For that reason, any score should be treated as a hint that calls for further review rather than as proof.

item.title: BestPhotoAI
item.description:
BestPhotoAI is meant for fast photo improvement. A user uploads an image, and the tool can sharpen details, increase resolution, fix lighting and color, and retouch skin, then returns an enhanced version. The aim is to save time compared with manual editing in Photoshop or Lightroom.

Typical users are e-commerce sellers who need clean product photos, creators preparing profile and social images, and people restoring older pictures. Automated enhancement works best on ordinary issues like low light or noise, and results vary with the source image.

item.title: Bing Image Creator
item.description: Bing Image Creator made AI image generation easy to try. You type a description, and it returns several images within a few seconds, with no installation and no cost beyond a Microsoft account. Its popularity came from being free and being available inside Bing and Edge, long before many alternatives had a free tier. Microsoft has since renamed the tool Image Creator from Designer and tied it into Copilot and the Designer app.

item.title: ClipDrop
item.description:
Clipdrop packages common image edits into simple web tools. Remove Background cuts out a subject in a click, Cleanup erases unwanted objects, Image Upscaler enlarges small pictures with added detail, and Uncrop extends an image beyond its borders. Relight changes the lighting on a subject, and Replace Background swaps in a new scene from a text prompt. A text-to-image generator rounds out the set, using Stability AI models.

Product photographers, e-commerce sellers, marketers, and casual users reach for it when they need a quick edit without opening a heavy editor. The tools work in the browser and on mobile, with an API for developers who want to add the same features to their own apps. The project had a short stint under Stability AI before moving to Jasper, which acquired it to expand its marketing tools.

item.title: Connected Papers
item.description: Connected Papers helps you get oriented in a research area. You enter a paper title, DOI, or link, and it produces a graph where each node is a paper and closer nodes are more similar. Similarity comes from co-citation and bibliographic coupling, meaning papers that cite similar sources or are cited together, rather than from keywords. Node size and color show citation count and year, which lets you see influential and recent work at a glance.

item.title: DALL-E 3
item.description:
DALL-E 3 was a text-to-image model known for following detailed prompts closely. Its integration with ChatGPT let users describe an image in conversation and have the assistant refine the prompt, which made image generation accessible to people who had never used a dedicated art tool. Developers could also call it through OpenAI’s API.

It was part of a line that began with the original DALL-E and DALL-E 2, which helped popularize text-to-image generation. Over time, OpenAI moved to newer image models built natively into its multimodal systems, which handle text in images and edits better. DALL-E branding faded as a result.

item.title: Dora
item.description:
Dora targets people who want a standout site without writing code. A user describes the site or starts from a template, and the platform generates pages with 3D objects, scroll animations, and interactions, which are expensive to build by hand. A visual editor lets them adjust layout, copy, and motion.

Designers and small businesses use it for portfolios, landing pages, and marketing sites where visual impact matters. Compared with simple builders, it emphasizes motion and depth. Published sites are hosted by the platform, and exporting options vary by plan.

item.title: Erase.bg
item.description:
Erase.bg handles one of the most common editing jobs. You upload a picture of a product, person, or object, and an AI model detects the foreground and removes the background, producing a PNG with transparency. It works on people, products, animals, and cars, and handles complex edges like hair reasonably well. Typical users are online sellers, designers, and anyone making a profile picture or a presentation.

Several features make it more practical for volume work. Batch processing lets you upload many images at once, and an API and plugins integrate with design tools and workflows. After removing the background, you can add a solid color, a new image, or leave it transparent. A free tier gives low-resolution results, and paid credits or subscriptions unlock high-resolution downloads.

item.title: Fliz
item.description:
Fliz focuses on one-click video creation. A user pastes a link or text, picks a style and voice, and Fliz writes a script if needed, assembles scenes, adds captions and music, and renders a video. The goal is a finished piece that can go straight to social media or a website.

Typical uses are turning blog posts into short videos, creating product videos for e-commerce, and producing news-style clips. Editing tools allow changes to visuals, text, and voices, and the platform supports many languages. Automation features generate videos in bulk from feeds.

item.title: Fotor
item.description:
Fotor covers everyday editing for people who do not want Photoshop.
