In the photo editor, you crop, adjust color and light, apply filters and effects, and retouch portraits by smoothing skin and removing blemishes. A collage maker and a design studio offer templates for social posts, posters, and cards. Everything works in a browser, with matching apps for phones and computers.

AI tools handle the harder steps. One-click enhancement improves exposure and sharpness, background removal makes cutouts, an object remover erases distractions, and an upscaler enlarges small pictures. Newer features include text-to-image generation, avatars, and generative fill for extending or changing parts of an image. Fotor also has an AI video editor for simple clips.

item.title: freebeat AI
item.description:
freebeat takes a different approach to video generation. A user uploads a track, and the platform produces visuals that follow the rhythm of the music, cutting and transforming on the beat. The result is a music-driven video that can be shared on social platforms.

Musicians use it to create lyric visuals and promotional clips without a video team. Creators use it for background visuals and short-form content. Styles and prompts guide the look, and users can adjust timing and effects.

item.title: Galileo AI
item.description:
Galileo AI was one of the early tools for turning a prompt into interface designs. You described a screen, such as a fitness app dashboard or a checkout page, and it produced a detailed, editable design with components, imagery, and layout, which could be copied into Figma and refined. It was popular with product designers and founders as a way to explore ideas and get past the blank canvas.

Google acquired Galileo AI and brought its team and technology into its own design-generation product, Stitch, which creates interfaces from text or images and exports to Figma and code. The standalone Galileo service was wound down as part of that move.

item.title: Hailuo AI
item.description:
Hailuo AI is the consumer face of video models from MiniMax, a Chinese AI company. You type a prompt or upload an image, and it generates a short video clip, with motion that many users find natural, including complex movement like dancing, sports, and camera moves. It gained a following among creators for the quality of its image-to-video results and its willingness to follow detailed prompts.

The platform offers tools for steering results. A subject reference feature keeps a character consistent across clips, camera controls guide movement, and different model versions trade speed for quality. It also generates images and offers voice and music features through MiniMax’s other models. An API lets developers use the video models in their own products.

item.title: Haiper
item.description:
Haiper launched as a fast, accessible video generator. Users typed a prompt or uploaded an image and received a short clip, with tools to extend videos, repaint areas, and animate stills. The company emphasized speed and iteration, aiming to let creators try many ideas quickly, and attracted attention as one of the more promising independent challengers to larger video model makers.

It could not keep pace with the rapid advances and heavy computing costs of video models. The company closed its consumer platform, and its founders moved to other roles, while its video models were acquired by another company that offers them through an API for enterprises. User projects hosted on the original platform were no longer accessible.

item.title: Ideogram
item.description:
Ideogram became known for solving a problem that frustrated early image generators: spelling. Ask most models for a poster that says “Grand Opening” and you get distorted letters, while Ideogram’s models usually produce clean, legible type in a chosen style. That makes it a practical choice for posters, book covers, t-shirt designs, logos, memes, and social media graphics, where words are part of the image.

It also performs well on general image generation, with strong prompt following across photorealistic, illustrated, and graphic design styles. Beyond generating from scratch, the apps include tools to remove backgrounds, erase objects, resize images for ads, and edit text layers. Teams can use private generation, shared libraries, and custom models, and a developer API provides the same models in other products.

item.title: InstaWebAI
item.description:
InstaWebAI generates a full website from a short brief. A user enters information about the business, and the tool creates pages, copy, images, and a structure designed for search engines, which can be edited and published. The goal is to cut the time from idea to live site to minutes.

It targets owners who lack design or writing skills and want a professional baseline. Typical outputs include home, services, about, and contact pages, along with metadata for search visibility. Publishing options and domain connections vary by plan.

item.title: Julius AI
item.description: Julius lets people explore data by asking questions. After uploading a CSV or Excel file, or connecting to a database or Google Sheets, you can ask for things like the average sales by region, a trend over time, or a correlation between two columns. Julius writes and runs code behind the scenes, then shows the result as a chart, a table, or a written explanation, and you can view the code to check what it did.

item.title: Kindroid
item.description:
Kindroid lets users create a companion from scratch. You write the character’s background and personality, choose how they look using generated images, and give them a voice, and then talk by text or voice calls. The app emphasizes memory, so the character can recall details from earlier conversations, and users can adjust how the AI responds by editing the character’s profile and diary.

Other features include group chats with several characters, image generation of the character in various scenes, and selfie sharing. Users value the high level of control and the more natural conversation compared with simpler chatbots. Some use it for roleplay and storytelling, others for companionship or practicing conversation.

item.title: Kling AI
item.description: Kling is the AI video product from Kuaishou, the Chinese short-video company behind the Kwai app. Its models generate clips from a text description or a starting image, and they are well regarded for natural motion, realistic physics, and faces and bodies that stay coherent through a shot. When it first appeared, it was one of the strongest challengers to Western video tools, and it has stayed in the top group as the field has moved quickly.

item.title: Krea AI
item.description:
Krea became popular for its real-time canvas. As you type a prompt or sketch shapes, the image updates almost instantly, which turns generation into a live, exploratory process instead of waiting for each result. That immediacy suits designers and artists who iterate visually, adjusting composition and style through gestures rather than rewriting prompts.

The platform has expanded into a wide creative toolkit. It lets you generate images and video with a selection of models from different providers, upscale and enhance images with a strong emphasis on detail, edit existing pictures, and train custom styles from your own examples. Features such as pattern and logo generation, and tools for animating stills, appeal to designers and motion artists. Multiple models in one place make comparison easy.

item.title: Leonardo AI
item.description:
Leonardo.ai began as a tool for game developers who needed lots of consistent assets. Users generate images from text prompts with a choice of Leonardo’s own models and others, then refine them with inpainting, upscaling, and background removal. Fine-tuned models for characters, environments, items, and concept art made it popular with game artists, illustrators, and designers who care about a particular visual style.

Customization is a major draw. You can train your own models on a set of images to produce consistent characters or brand looks, use reference images to control composition and style, and draw on a canvas to guide generation. The platform has added video generation and animation of stills, along with an API for developers. A community feed lets users see what others are making and borrow prompts.

item.title: Litmaps
item.description: Litmaps helps researchers see a field instead of reading a list. You start with one or more papers you know, and the tool plots them on a map where one axis shows publication date and the other shows how much a paper is cited. Lines between the nodes show citation links. From the seeds, it suggests related papers that cite or are cited by your set, so you can quickly find missing foundational works and recent developments.

item.title: Luma Dream Machine
item.description: Dream Machine is how most people first used Luma AI’s video models. You describe a scene or upload a still image, and it produces a short clip with motion, lighting, and camera movement that tends to look cinematic. Luma started as a 3D capture company, which still shows in how well its video models handle depth and camera moves. People use it for concept videos, storyboards, social content, product shots, and b-roll when a shoot is not practical.

item.title: MagicLight
item.description:
MagicLight is designed for narrative video. A user writes or pastes a story or script, chooses a style, and the platform produces scenes with characters, backgrounds, narration, and music. The aim is to let people who cannot animate create short animated stories and explainers.

It is used for children’s stories, educational content, social media series, and marketing videos. Features such as consistent characters across scenes help with storytelling, and editing tools allow changes to scenes and text before export.

item.title: Meshy
item.description:
Meshy makes 3D asset creation fast. You type a description or upload an image, and it generates a 3D mesh with textures in a minute or two. The results can be rotated, refined, and downloaded in common formats. Indie game developers, 3D printing hobbyists, product designers, and virtual world builders use it to produce props, characters, and environment pieces without modeling each from scratch.

The platform includes tools for the steps after generation. It can retexture a model from a prompt, remesh to adjust polygon counts and topology, and add skeletons and animations to characters. Plugins and an API connect it with Blender, Unity, Unreal Engine, Maya, and other tools, so assets can flow into existing pipelines. A library of community models provides starting points.

item.title: Noodle Tomato
item.description:
Noodle Tomato targets faceless channel creators. A user enters a topic, and the tool writes a script, generates or selects visuals, adds a voiceover, and assembles a video that can be uploaded to YouTube. The aim is to make it possible to publish regularly with little production effort.

This style of content has drawn scrutiny. YouTube has policies against mass-produced, repetitive, or low-value videos, and channels that rely on automation without adding original value can lose monetization. Quality depends on editing, fact-checking, and a clear perspective.

item.title: NovelAI
item.description: NovelAI started as a tool for writers who wanted an AI collaborator for fiction. In its editor, you write a passage and the AI continues it, with controls for style, memory, and the characters and world in your story. Features such as lorebooks store details about characters and places so the AI keeps them consistent, and you can edit, retry, and steer the output freely. It’s used by hobbyist novelists, roleplayers, and fan fiction writers.

item.title: Obsidian AI
item.description:
Obsidian’s approach to AI follows its general philosophy: keep the core simple and let users choose add-ons. Because notes are plain files in a folder, they work well with language models. Community plugins let you chat with your vault, ask questions about your notes, summarize long documents, rewrite text, and find related notes by meaning instead of keywords. Smart Connections and Copilot-style plugins are popular examples.

Users have a lot of freedom over where the AI runs. A plugin can send text to a hosted model like those from OpenAI, Anthropic, or Google using your own API key, or it can connect to a local model through tools such as Ollama or LM Studio, so notes never leave your computer. Some people also expose their vault to coding agents and assistants through the Model Context Protocol, which lets tools like Claude read and organize notes.

item.title: Outfit.fm
item.description:
Outfit.fm addresses the cost of fashion photography. A seller photographs a garment on a hanger or flat, uploads it, and the tool generates images of the item on virtual models in settings that suit the brand. Options include different body types, poses, and backgrounds.

Small brands and online sellers use it to fill catalogs and social feeds without booking models, studios, and photographers. Speed lets them test styles and update visuals frequently.

item.title: Photoroom
item.description:
Photoroom grew from a background remover into a full product photography tool. Take a picture of a product on a table, and the app cuts it out cleanly, then places it on a white background, a color, or an AI-generated scene with realistic shadows and lighting. For small sellers on marketplaces like Etsy, eBay, and Shopify, that means professional-looking listings without a studio.

Other features expand the range. An AI backgrounds tool creates settings from a text description, an instant shadow and relight tool adds depth, and a magic retouch removes objects and blemishes. Templates in standard sizes speed up posts for social media and marketplaces. Batch editing handles whole catalogs, and an API lets platforms add the same processing to their own apps. Teams can share brand templates.

item.title: PixVerse
item.description:
PixVerse turns prompts and images into video. Users describe a scene or upload a picture, choose a style, and receive a clip. Templates and effects support social content, and features like character consistency and lip sync help with storytelling.

The platform also provides editing, extension, and animation of still images, and offers apps for mobile and web. It is popular among social creators for fast, trend-driven formats.

PixVerse has a free tier with credits and paid plans. Output length and realism have limits, and rights depend on plan terms. Alternatives include Pika, Runway, Kling, Luma, and Higgsfield. PixVerse suits creators making quick AI videos.

item.title: Predis.ai
item.description: Predis.ai aims to make social content creation quick for small businesses and creators. You enter a prompt or paste a link to your product page or website, choose a format such as a single image, carousel, or short video, and the tool generates a post with a caption, hashtags, and a branded design. Editing tools let you change the text, images, and layout, and apply your brand colors and logo.

item.title: Remove.bg
item.description:
Remove.bg made background removal fast and easy. You upload a photo, or drag it onto the page, and an AI model detects the foreground and returns the image with a transparent background in a few seconds. It handles people, products, animals, and cars, and it copes reasonably well with difficult edges like hair and fur. It is used for e-commerce product photos, profile pictures, ID photos, and design mockups.

The service extends beyond the website. Plugins connect it to Photoshop, Figma, and other tools, apps let you process images on a phone or desktop, and an API allows platforms to add automatic background removal at scale. Once the background is removed, you can add a solid color, a template, or another image. Bulk tools handle large catalogs. Remove.bg is owned by Canva.

item.title: Replicate
item.description: Replicate makes it easy to use machine learning models without managing servers. A developer picks a model from a large public library, such as an image generator, a speech tool, a video model, or a language model, and calls it through a few lines of code. The platform handles GPUs, scaling, and versioning, and charges by the second of compute, so costs track real use. Many hobbyist and startup apps rely on it.

item.title: The Influencer AI
item.description:
The Influencer AI generates a virtual person who can appear in ads, product demos, and social posts. A brand creates or selects a character and the tool produces images and videos of that character holding products, talking to the camera, or appearing in scenes, with consistent looks across content.

The pitch is cost and speed. Producing varied creative with real models requires scheduling, travel, and fees, while AI can generate many variations quickly for testing ads. Features include scripts, voices, and lip-synced video.

item.title: ThumbnailCreator.com
item.description:
ThumbnailCreator targets one chore. A creator describes the thumbnail they want or uploads a frame from a video, and the tool produces several thumbnail options with text, backgrounds, and subjects arranged to catch attention.

Because thumbnails strongly affect click rates, creators iterate on them often. A generator that makes variations lets them test ideas without opening a design program each time.

Independent information is limited. ThumbnailCreator has a free tier and paid plans. Alternatives include Canva, Photoroom, VidIQ and TubeBuddy thumbnail tools, Midjourney, and hiring a designer. ThumbnailCreator suits YouTubers who make many thumbnails.

item.title: Tripo3D
item.description:
Tripo focuses on speed and consistency. Enter a description or upload an image, and it generates a 3D model in seconds to a minute, with options for style and level of detail. The models are meant to be usable in games, animation, 3D printing, and e-commerce, and the platform provides downloads in common formats like GLB, FBX, and OBJ.

Features go beyond the initial generation. Tools can create cleaner topology for animation, generate or replace textures from a prompt, add skeletons so characters can be posed, and apply animations. A segmentation option separates a model into parts for editing. An API and integrations with Blender, Unity, Unreal, and other applications fit it into creative pipelines, and a community library offers starting points.

item.title: Uizard
item.description:
Uizard is a design tool built for speed and accessibility. You can upload a photo of a sketch or a screenshot of an existing app and have it converted into an editable design, or describe a screen in text and let the AI generate a layout. A library of templates, components, and themes helps non-designers build presentable prototypes for products, websites, and apps.

Collaboration features let teams comment and iterate, and prototypes can be linked into clickable flows. An Autodesigner feature creates multi-screen designs from a prompt, and the AI can generate color themes from an image. It’s popular with founders, product managers, and consultants who need quick mockups to communicate ideas.

item.title: VidFlux
item.description:
VidFlux takes a still image and brings it to life. A user uploads a photo, optionally describes the motion, and the tool generates a short video with movement such as camera pans, flowing hair, or moving water.

Marketers use it to give product photos life in ads and social feeds, and creators animate portraits and artwork. The clips are short and quality varies with the image.

Independent information is limited. VidFlux has a free tier and paid plans. Alternatives include Runway, Pika, Luma, Kling, and PixVerse. VidFlux suits creators animating still images.

item.title: Wan Video
item.description:
Wan generates video from descriptions. Users provide a prompt or an image, and the model produces a clip with motion and detail. Alibaba has released several versions, including open-weight models that run on local hardware and have attracted a large community of tools and fine-tunes.

Creators and filmmakers use Wan for text-to-video, image-to-video, and editing tasks, through hosted sites and through open-source workflows such as ComfyUI. Open availability makes it a base for research and custom pipelines.

item.title: Weights & Biases
item.description:
Weights & Biases, often shortened to W&B, grew out of a simple need. Machine learning engineers run many experiments with different settings and want to compare them. By adding a few lines of code to a training script, you log metrics, hyperparameters, system usage, and sample outputs to a dashboard, and see runs side by side with charts and tables. That replaces scattered notebooks and spreadsheets.

The platform has grown beyond tracking. Artifacts version datasets and models so you can trace what produced a result, Sweeps automate hyperparameter searches, Reports let teams share findings, and a model registry supports handoff to deployment. Weave covers LLM apps with tracing and evaluation, and W&B Inference offers hosted model access.
